question: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption, and where does this password manager use each?
answer_hinglish:
Symmetric encryption mein encrypt aur decrypt dono same key se hote hain -- fast hota hai, bulk data ke liye perfect. Asymmetric mein do alag keys hoti hain: public key (sabko de sakte ho) encrypt karti hai, private key (sirf owner ke paas) decrypt karti hai -- slow hota hai aur sirf chhota payload encrypt kar sakta hai.

Is project mein dono use hote hain, alag-alag jagah. Vault ka har entry aur canary AES-256-GCM se encrypt hota hai -- yeh symmetric hai, same derived key encrypt aur decrypt dono karti hai (`src/crypto.ts`). Lekin sharing feature mein, jab alice apna entry dave ke vault ko bhejti hai, tab RSA-OAEP (asymmetric) use hota hai -- par poora entry RSA se encrypt nahi hota, sirf ek one-time AES key RSA se wrap hoti hai (`src/sharing.ts::sealForRecipient`), aur actual data wahi purani AES-GCM se encrypt hota hai.

Yeh combination hybrid/envelope encryption kehlata hai -- interview mein yeh hi expect hota hai jab bolo 'RSA slow hai, bulk data ke liye nahi'. Alice ko kabhi dave ki private key nahi dikhti, aur dave ko alice ka master password ya vault key kabhi nahi dikhta -- dono taraf se independent crypto hai.
why_needed: Interviewer yeh dekhna chahta hai ki tumhe pata hai konsa algorithm kab use karna hai -- symmetric fast hai par key share karna mushkil, asymmetric key-sharing solve karta hai par slow aur size-limited hai.
real_world_analogy: Symmetric: ek hi ghar ki chaabi se dono darwaza khulta aur band hota hai. Asymmetric: tumhara letterbox slot (public, koi bhi daal sakta hai) aur uski chaabi (sirf tumhare paas, sirf tum khol sakte ho) -- dono alag hain.
how_it_works: crypto.ts mein `encrypt(key, plaintext)` aur `decrypt(key, blob)` same `key` Buffer leti hain -- symmetric. sharing.ts mein `sealForRecipient` public key se sirf AES key wrap karti hai, `openAsRecipient` private key se unwrap karti hai -- asymmetric sirf ek chhoti key ke liye.
in_this_project: `src/crypto.ts::encrypt` aur `decrypt` har entry aur canary ke liye symmetric AES-256-GCM. `src/sharing.ts::generateSharingKeyPair` RSA-2048 keypair banata hai; `sealForRecipient` aur `openAsRecipient` sirf one-time AES key ko wrap/unwrap karte hain asymmetric se.
code_example:
// real, src/sharing.ts sealForRecipient (trimmed)
const oneTimeKey = randomBytes(32); // AES-256, symmetric
const blob = encrypt(oneTimeKey, plaintext); // symmetric: fast, any size
const wrappedKey = publicEncrypt({ key: recipientPublicKeyPem, ...RSA_OPTIONS }, oneTimeKey); // asymmetric: only the small key
advantages: Symmetric: bulk data ke liye fast
Asymmetric: key-exchange problem solve karta hai, dono taraf private key share nahi karni padti
Hybrid combination dono ke fayde deta hai
disadvantages: Asymmetric akela use karte toh entry ka size limit hota (RSA-2048 bahut chhota payload encrypt kar sakti hai)
Symmetric akela use karte toh key kaise safely dusre vault tak pahunchaate, yeh problem reh jaati
common_mistakes: RSA se seedha poora entry encrypt karne ki koshish karna (payload size limit se fail hoga)
Symmetric key ko kisi tarah plaintext mein transmit karna
Dono ko ek hi cheez samajh lena
follow_up_questions: Why can RSA not directly encrypt a whole vault entry?
What happens if the recipient's public key is invalid?
Why is a fresh one-time AES key generated for every share instead of reusing one?

question: What is the fundamental difference between hashing and encryption, and where does each actually get used in this project?
answer_hinglish:
Hashing one-way hai -- ek baar hash ban gaya, usse original value wapas nahi nikal sakte (sirf guess karke verify kar sakte ho). Encryption two-way hai -- jiske paas key hai woh ciphertext ko plaintext mein wapas la sakta hai. Yeh basic difference bahut important hai kyunki galat jagah galat primitive use karna seedha security hole bana deta hai.

Is project mein dono alag jagah use hote hain, aur dono ki jagah deliberate hai. Master password KABHI hash nahi hota -- usse ek "canary" encrypt kiya jaata hai (two-way, kyunki verify karne ke liye decrypt karna hai, PLAN.md mein likha hai "one KDF, one artifact, no second hash field"). Breach-check feature mein password ka SHA-1 HASH liya jaata hai (`sha1Hex`), kyunki wahan sirf "yeh password kisi breach database mein hai ya nahi" compare karna hai -- original password wapas chahiye hi nahi, sirf irreversible fingerprint chahiye jo kisi doosre service ko bina password bheje compare ho sake.

Agar master password hash hota (jaise ek normal login system karta hai), toh verification ke liye koi dusra artifact chahiye hota -- par yahan canary approach se ek hi KDF output (derived key) se encrypt aur verify dono ho jaate hain, isliye hash ki zaroorat hi nahi padi.
why_needed: Confuse karna common mistake hai -- bahut log sochte hain password "hash" hota hai har jagah, par yahan verification ke liye encryption use hota hai aur breach-check ke liye hashing, dono ka purpose alag hai.
real_world_analogy: Hashing jaise ek blender mein fruit daal kar juice bana dena -- juice se wapas poora fruit nahi bana sakte, sirf match kar sakte ho ki "haan yeh us fruit ka juice tha". Encryption jaise fruit ko lock box mein dalna -- chaabi ho toh wapas poora fruit nikal sakte ho.
how_it_works: `src/breach.ts::sha1Hex` -> `createHash("sha1").update(input).digest("hex")` -- one-way. `src/crypto.ts::encrypt`/`decrypt` -- AES-256-GCM, key ke saath reversible. `verifyMasterPassword` canary ko decrypt karti hai, hash compare nahi karti.
in_this_project: `src/manager.ts::CANARY_PLAINTEXT` ek fixed string hai jo har vault creation par encrypt hoti hai, master password kabhi stored/hashed nahi hota. `src/breach.ts::sha1Hex` password ka SHA-1 leti hai sirf breach-check ke liye, aur sirf pehle 5 characters bhejte hain (k-anonymity).
advantages: Canary approach: ek hi artifact verification ke liye, no separate hash to keep in sync
Hashing breach-check ke liye sahi primitive hai kyunki reversibility ki zaroorat hi nahi
disadvantages: Agar koi dev galti se master password ko bhi hash karne ki koshish kare, toh verification flow todna padega
SHA-1 cryptographically weak hai collision attacks ke against, par yahan sirf k-anonymity bucketing ke liye use ho raha hai (same protocol HIBP use karta hai), password verification ke liye nahi
common_mistakes: Master password ko hash karke store karna (yahan use hi nahi hua)
Breach-check ke liye encryption use karna jab hashing hi kaafi hai
Yeh sochna ki hashing bhi "decrypt" ho sakti hai
follow_up_questions: Why is SHA-1 acceptable here when it is considered weak for other purposes?
Why does the canary use encryption instead of a stored hash?
What would break if someone replaced sha1Hex with encrypt/decrypt in breach.ts?

question: What is a cryptographic salt, and what specific attack does it defend against in this project?
answer_hinglish:
Salt ek random value hai jo KDF (key derivation function) ko password ke saath mix karte hain, taaki same password alag-alag jagah same key na bana de. Isse rainbow table attack rukta hai -- attacker precomputed hash/key table bana leta hai common passwords ke liye, par salt se woh table useless ho jaata hai kyunki har vault ka apna unique salt hai.

Is project mein `newSalt()` function `randomBytes(16)` se 16-byte random salt banata hai, jo `createVault` ke time generate hota hai aur vault ke saath permanently store hota hai (plaintext mein, salt secret nahi hota). `deriveKey(masterPassword, salt)` scrypt ko password AUR salt dono deta hai. Test `crypto.test.ts` mein directly prove hota hai: "a different salt (or a different password) produces a different key" -- same password, alag salt, alag key.

Practical impact: agar do users same master password "correct-horse-battery" use karein, dono ke vault ka derived key BILKUL alag hoga, kyunki unka salt alag hai. Isliye koi bhi attacker jo ek vault todne mein kaafi compute laga chuka hai, woh same precomputed work doosre vault par reuse nahi kar sakta -- har vault apna independent brute-force target ban jaata hai.
why_needed: Bina salt, same password = same key, jo precomputed attacks ko bahut easy bana deta hai aur ek leaked dataset se saare same-password users exposed ho jaate hain ek saath.
real_world_analogy: Har ghar ke lock ko thoda alag design (ek random pattern) de do, chahe sabke paas same key-word ho -- ab ek chaabi-master-copy banane se sab ghar nahi khulte, har ghar ka pattern unique hai.
how_it_works: `newSalt()` returns `randomBytes(SALT_LENGTH)` (16 bytes). `deriveKey` is `scryptSync(masterPassword, salt, KEY_LENGTH)`. Salt stored alongside the vault (and in `exportVault`/`PersistedVault`), not secret, not hashed.
in_this_project: `src/crypto.ts::newSalt` aur `SALT_LENGTH`. `createVault` mein ek baar generate hota hai; `changeMasterPassword` ek NAYA salt generate karta hai har rotation par. `test/crypto.test.ts` ki `deriveKey` describe block mein dono assertions hain.
advantages: Rainbow table attacks useless ho jaate hain
Same password, alag vaults -- koi correlation nahi
Salt secret nahi hai, store karna aasan hai
disadvantages: Salt khud password ko strong nahi banata -- weak password ab bhi weak hai, sirf precomputation attack slow hota hai
changeMasterPassword par naya salt generate hota hai, toh old aur new salt dono thoda extra bookkeeping maangte hain
common_mistakes: Salt ko secret maan kar encrypt karne ki koshish karna (zaroorat nahi hai)
Har user ke liye same global salt use karna
Salt ko hash karna instead of sirf store karna
follow_up_questions: Why is the salt allowed to be stored in plaintext?
What happens on changeMasterPassword to the salt?
Would a shorter salt (say 4 bytes) still be safe?

question: What is an IV in AES-GCM, and why is reusing one under the same key such a serious problem?
answer_hinglish:
IV (initialization vector, yahan 12 bytes, GCM ke liye recommended length) ek random value hai jo encrypt karte waqt key ke saath mix hoti hai, taaki SAME plaintext, SAME key se encrypt karne par bhi HAR baar alag ciphertext bane. Bina IV ke, same data dobara encrypt karne par identical ciphertext aata, jisse attacker pattern dekh sakta ("yeh dono entries same hain" jaise leak).

GCM mode mein IV reuse normal cipher se bhi zyada dangerous hai -- yeh sirf confidentiality nahi todta, balki agar attacker do ciphertexts dekhle jo same key+IV se bane hain, toh woh authentication key hi derive kar sakta hai aur phir kisi bhi message ko forge kar sakta hai, bina real key jaane. Isliye README mein likha hai: "Reusing an IV under the same key is the ONE way to badly break AES-GCM".

Is project mein `encrypt()` function har call par `randomBytes(IV_LENGTH)` se fresh IV generate karta hai -- chahe `addEntry` ho, `updateEntry` ho (jo entry ko re-encrypt karta hai), ya `changeMasterPassword` ki bulk re-encryption, har ek call apna naya IV leti hai. Test "uses a fresh IV each call" exactly yeh verify karta hai: same plaintext twice encrypt karo, dono ka `iv` field alag hona chahiye. Mutation K2 ("encrypt reuses a fixed IV") specifically isi invariant ko todne ki koshish thi, aur pakdi gayi.
why_needed: Agar IV repeat ho jaaye same key ke saath, toh attacker sirf pattern matching nahi, balki actual forgery kar sakta hai GCM mode mein -- yeh ek silent, catastrophic break hai, slow degradation nahi.
real_world_analogy: Ek hi letter ko har baar bilkul same tarike se fold karke bhejna vs har baar thoda different fold pattern use karna -- koi dekh le ki dono letters SAME tarike se folded hain toh samajh jaayega yeh connected hain, chahe content na pad sake.
how_it_works: `encrypt(key, plaintext)`: `const iv = randomBytes(IV_LENGTH)` har call par, phir `createCipheriv(ALGORITHM, key, iv)`. IV blob ke saath (plaintext, not secret) store hota hai taaki decrypt use kar sake.
in_this_project: `src/crypto.ts::encrypt` (`IV_LENGTH = 12`). `test/crypto.test.ts` "uses a fresh IV each call: encrypting the same plaintext twice never produces the same ciphertext". README's rules list: "a fresh random IV every time it is written (including on updateEntry)".
advantages: Fresh IV guarantees semantic security: identical plaintexts never look identical as ciphertext
No manual IV-tracking/counter needed -- random is simple and correct at this scale
disadvantages: Random IV relies on a good source of randomness (node:crypto's randomBytes, which is fine); a bad RNG would reintroduce the risk
IV itself must be stored/transmitted alongside ciphertext (small overhead, 12 bytes per blob)
common_mistakes: Caching or hardcoding an IV for 'performance'
Deriving the IV from a counter without guaranteeing it never resets
Assuming IV needs to be secret (it does not, only unique)
follow_up_questions: Why 12 bytes specifically for the IV, not 16?
What would an attacker actually be able to do if two blobs shared an IV and key?
Why does updateEntry re-encrypt with a brand new IV instead of reusing the entry's existing one?

question: What is a KDF, and why is scrypt deliberately slow instead of being made as fast as possible?
answer_hinglish:
KDF (key derivation function) ek low-entropy input (jaise human-chosen master password) leta hai aur usse ek fixed-length cryptographic key banata hai jo AES jaise cipher mein directly use ho sake. Lekin yeh job sirf ek "transform" nahi hai -- jab input master password hai jo guessable ho sakta hai, KDF ka doosra zaroori kaam hai attacker ke liye brute-force guessing ko EXPENSIVE banana.

scrypt deliberately slow aur memory-hard design kiya gaya hai: iske default cost parameters (N=16384, r=8, p=1) har ek derivation ko kuch milliseconds leta hai aur roughly 16 MiB memory use karta hai. Ek legit user ke liye yeh cost negligible hai -- woh ek baar unlock karte waqt pay karta hai. Par ek attacker jo offline lakhon passwords guess kar raha hai (jaise ek stolen `exportVault` se), use HAR guess ke liye yeh same cost pay karna padta hai -- jo brute-force ko practically bahut slow bana deta hai compared agar koi fast hash (jaise plain SHA-256) use hota.

Comment in `crypto.ts` explicitly yeh bolta hai: "Deliberately synchronous and deliberately slow... A real attacker guessing passwords offline pays this cost for every guess; a real user pays it once per unlock." Yeh ek asymmetric cost trade-off hai -- legit use case par minimal friction, attacker ke use case par maximum friction, same function se.
why_needed: Master password ka entropy limited hota hai (log yaad rakhne layak passwords chunte hain), toh offline guessing feasible hoti hai agar key derivation fast ho. Slow KDF guessing ko computationally expensive bana deta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek bank locker jiska combination check karne mein 3 second lagte hain (legit owner ke liye koi farq nahi) -- par ek thief jo sab combinations try kar raha hai, usse lakhon combinations x 3 second lagenge, jo practically impossible ho jaata hai.
how_it_works: `deriveKey(masterPassword, salt)` = `scryptSync(masterPassword, salt, KEY_LENGTH)`, synchronous call, Node's default scrypt cost params. Called on every `createVault`, `unlock`, and `changeMasterPassword`'s old+new password check.
in_this_project: `src/crypto.ts::deriveKey`, `KEY_LENGTH = 32` (AES-256). Called from `manager.ts::verifyMasterPassword` (unlock path) and `createVault`/`changeMasterPassword` (new password path). The comment above `deriveKey` explains the deliberate slowness directly in the source.
advantages: Legit per-unlock cost negligible, attacker's total guessing cost multiplied by number of guesses
Memory-hardness also resists cheap parallel GPU/ASIC brute-force, not just raw CPU time
Built into node:crypto, no third-party dependency
disadvantages: Slow KDF adds real latency to every unlock -- a UX cost, though small
Cost parameters are not currently tunable/configurable per deployment in this project
common_mistakes: Using a fast hash (SHA-256/MD5) directly as a KDF for a password
Reducing scrypt's cost parameters to 'speed things up' without realizing the security trade-off
Deriving the key once and caching it across unrelated vaults
follow_up_questions: What is the difference between scrypt, bcrypt, and Argon2, and would any of them be a better fit here?
Why is scrypt called synchronously rather than with an async variant?
What happens to unlock latency if KEY_LENGTH or the cost parameters were increased?

question: What does AEAD mean, and what exactly does the authentication tag protect against in this codebase?
answer_hinglish:
AEAD matlab Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data -- yeh ek primitive confidentiality (koi tumhara data padh nahi sakta bina key ke) AUR integrity/authenticity (koi tumhara data badal nahi sakta bina pakde jaane ke) dono ek saath deta hai. AES-256-GCM ek AEAD cipher hai: encrypt karte waqt ek `authTag` generate hota hai, aur decrypt karte waqt woh tag verify hota hai -- agar match na ho, decryption FAIL hota hai, kuch garbage return nahi hota.

Practically iska matlab hai: wrong key se decrypt karo, ya ciphertext/IV/authTag mein se kuch bhi tamper karo baad mein, result same hai -- `decrypt()` ek exception throw karta hai jo `PasswordManagerError("DECRYPTION_FAILED", ...)` mein convert ho jaata hai. GCM khud yeh differentiate NAHI karta ki galti kis wajah se hui -- comment code mein likha hai "GCM cannot tell these apart, and does not need to" -- security ke liye sirf yeh important hai ki EK consistent signal mile "yeh fail hua", chahe reason kuch bhi ho.

Yeh exact property hi master-password verification ka core mechanism banata hai (canary approach): koi separate hash-compare nahi likhna padta, AES-GCM ka built-in authentication check hi "sahi password" vs "galat password" ka decision le leta hai. Test suite isi property ko teen tarah se verify karta hai -- wrong key, tampered ciphertext, tampered authTag, tampered IV -- sab `DECRYPTION_FAILED` dete hain.
why_needed: Bina authentication, encrypted data silently tamper ho sakta hai aur decrypt ho kar galat (par syntactically valid-looking) plaintext de sakta hai -- attacker ciphertext modify karke application ko confuse kar sakta hai. AEAD yeh poora class of attack rokta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek sealed envelope jisme tamper-evident seal lagi ho -- agar koi raaste mein letter khol kar wapas band kare, seal tootne ka saboot mil jaata hai; receiver letter padhta hi nahi jab tak seal intact na ho.
how_it_works: `encrypt()`: `cipher.getAuthTag()` se authTag milta hai ciphertext ke saath. `decrypt()`: `decipher.setAuthTag(authTag)` phir `decipher.final()` -- yahi line throw karti hai agar tag match na ho, catch block mein `DECRYPTION_FAILED` ban jaata hai.
in_this_project: `src/crypto.ts::EncryptedBlob` (`iv`, `ciphertext`, `authTag` teeno fields). `decrypt()` ka try/catch. `test/crypto.test.ts`: "decrypting with the wrong key throws DECRYPTION_FAILED", "a ciphertext altered after encryption fails authentication", "an altered authTag fails authentication", "an altered IV fails authentication". Mutation K3 ("decrypt never checks the auth tag") exactly isi ko todne ki koshish thi.
advantages: One primitive gives both confidentiality and tamper-detection, no separate HMAC needed
Master password verification piggybacks on this for free (the canary mechanism)
A single consistent error regardless of exact tamper reason -- no information leak about WHY it failed
disadvantages: If the IV is ever reused with the same key, GCM's authentication guarantee itself breaks down (see the IV question)
Error message deliberately does not distinguish wrong-key from tampered-data, which can make debugging a real bug (not an attack) slightly harder
common_mistakes: Using a non-AEAD mode (plain AES-CBC) and bolting on a separate, easy-to-get-wrong MAC
Catching the decrypt exception and silently returning something instead of propagating DECRYPTION_FAILED
Assuming a failed auth-tag check means specifically 'wrong password' rather than any kind of tamper
follow_up_questions: Why does decrypt() throw one generic error instead of separate codes for 'wrong key' vs 'tampered data'?
What is the difference between AES-GCM and AES-CBC-HMAC in terms of what AEAD gives you for free?
How does this authentication tag check end up being the master-password verification mechanism?

question: What does k-anonymity mean in the context of breach checking, and how does this project implement it without ever sending the real password or full hash?
answer_hinglish:
k-anonymity ka matlab hai: jo response tumhe milta hai, usme tumhara real data kam se kam k-1 doosre entries ke saath INDISTINGUISHABLE hai -- koi observer sirf response dekh kar yeh nahi bata sakta ki tumhara ASLI value kaunsa tha. Have I Been Pwned ka real password API yehi protocol use karta hai, aur yeh project usi protocol ko fake data ke saath implement karta hai.

Flow hai: password ka SHA-1 hash lo (`sha1Hex`), uske pehle 5 hex characters "prefix" bano, baaki 35 characters "suffix" bane. `provider.lookupPrefix(prefix, signal)` ko sirf yeh 5-char prefix bheja jaata hai -- provider us prefix ke SAARE breached hashes ke suffixes return karta hai (ek set, jisme tumhara wala bhi hoga agar breached hai, aur kai dusre unrelated passwords ke suffixes bhi honge). Phir comparison -- "kya mera suffix is list mein hai?" -- LOCALLY, `isPasswordBreached` function mein hota hai, provider ko kabhi pata nahi chalta tumhara asli password ya hash kya tha.

Yeh property specifically test hoti hai: `test/breach.test.ts` ek spy provider use karta hai yeh prove karne ke liye ki `lookupPrefix` ko kabhi 5 characters se zyada kuch nahi jaata, aur definitely password ya full hash nahi. Mutation BR2 ("6-character prefix sent instead of 5") exactly isi anonymity-guarantee ko todne ki koshish thi -- agar prefix ek character bhi lamba ho jaaye, bucket size kam ho jaata hai aur anonymity weaker ho jaati hai.
why_needed: Breach-check ke liye ek third-party service ko apna password (ya uska full hash) bhejna khud ek bada risk hai -- us service ko ab tumhara actual password/hash pata chal jaata. k-anonymity yeh risk eliminate karta hai while still useful info de kar.
real_world_analogy: Doctor ko apna poora medical record dikhane ke bajaye, sirf apni age-group aur city batana ("30-40 saal, Mumbai mein kitne log yeh symptom rakhte hain") -- woh ek useful statistic de sakta hai bina tumhe specifically identify kiye.
how_it_works: `isPasswordBreached(password, provider, signal)`: `hash = sha1Hex(password)`, `prefix = hash.slice(0,5)`, `suffix = hash.slice(5)`, `suffixes = await provider.lookupPrefix(prefix, signal)`, return `suffixes.includes(suffix)`. Comparison local hai, provider ko sirf prefix milta hai.
in_this_project: `src/breach.ts::isPasswordBreached`, `sha1Hex`, `FakeBreachProvider::lookupPrefix`. `test/breach.test.ts`: "sha1Hex matches a well-known public value", "never sends more than a 5-character prefix, never the password or the full hash" (spy provider test).
advantages: Real password or full hash never leaves the caller
Same protocol a real-world, widely trusted service (HIBP) actually uses
Provider can still be useful (returns real matching data) without learning the query
disadvantages: Provider still learns the prefix and request timing/IP, which combined with other signals could narrow things down over many queries
SHA-1 is weak against collision attacks generally, though that is not the property being relied on here
common_mistakes: Sending the full hash instead of just the 5-character prefix (defeats the anonymity set)
Sending the plaintext password directly to the provider
Doing the suffix comparison on the provider's side instead of locally
follow_up_questions: Why 5 hex characters specifically, and not 3 or 8?
What is OPRF, and how does HIBP's real v3 API improve on plain k-anonymity?
What could a malicious provider still learn even while honoring the k-anonymity protocol correctly?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: 5-char prefix protocol ek trade-off hai: security (full hash/password kabhi nahi jaata) ke against provider ka load badh jaata hai, kyunki ek prefix bucket mein typically bahut saare unrelated hashes hote hain (16^5 = roughly 1 million possible buckets total), toh provider ko exact match ke bajaye ek pura bucket return karna padta hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar provider request logs (prefix + IP + timestamp) ko time ke saath correlate kare, toh kai queries milakar password-family guess karna theoretically possible hai -- isliye k-anonymity akela complete privacy guarantee nahi deta, sirf single-query ke level par anonymity deta hai.
advanced.alternatives: Private set intersection (PSI), OPRF-based blinded queries (jo HIBP ka real v3 API use karta hai, stronger guarantee deta hai), ya ek static downloadable full breached-password dataset jo client locally check kare bina kisi network call ke.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Zyada scale par, common/weak passwords ke prefixes bahut frequently query honge -- un hot prefixes ke suffix-lists ko caching layer mein rakhna provider ka load kam karega; HIBP khud bahut high volume ke liye poora dataset download allow karta hai instead of per-query API.
advanced.production_improvements: Ek real network-based provider wire karna retries aur caching ke saath, prefix-level response caching with a TTL, aur eventually OPRF-based protocol migrate karna agar stronger privacy guarantee chahiye plain k-anonymity se.

question: How does the master-password 'canary' mechanism verify a password is correct without the master password ever being stored anywhere, even as a hash?
answer_hinglish:
Canary approach ka idea simple hai: master password itself ya uska hash KABHI store nahi hota -- bas ek random salt aur ek "canary" (fixed plaintext ciphertext) store hota hai. Vault creation ke time, `CANARY_PLAINTEXT` (ek fixed string `"password-manager-canary-v1"`) ko derive ki gayi key se encrypt kar diya jaata hai, aur sirf yeh ciphertext (iv + authTag ke saath) store hoti hai.

Unlock karte waqt, entered password se salt ke saath EK naya candidate key derive hota hai (`deriveKey`), aur phir woh candidate key se canary ko decrypt karne ki koshish hoti hai. Agar password sahi tha, candidate key exactly wahi original key hogi, decrypt successfully `CANARY_PLAINTEXT` wapas de dega. Agar password galat tha, candidate key kuch aur hogi, aur AES-GCM ka authentication tag verification automatically FAIL ho jaayega -- `decrypt()` exception throw karta hai, jo `verifyMasterPassword` ke catch block mein `INVALID_MASTER_PASSWORD` ban jaata hai.

Yeh elegant hai kyunki verification ka POORA logic AES-GCM ke built-in auth-tag check par depend karta hai -- koi separate "compare hash" step nahi likhna padta. PLAN.md mein yeh decision explicitly justify hai: "One KDF, one artifact, no second 'password hash' field that could drift out of sync with it" -- matlab agar do separate secrets (hash + something else) rakhte, woh dono sync mein rehna chahiye; canary approach mein sirf ek hi cheez hai jo verify karna padta hai.
why_needed: Password manager ko real master password ever retain nahi karna chahiye, chahe hashed form mein bhi -- canary approach se verification ke liye koi separate secret maintain nahi karna padta, aur wahi mechanism key derivation ka bhi kaam karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek locked diary jisme ek fixed, famous quote likha hota hai (jaise koi standard first page). Diary khulti hai ya nahi, ispar hi tum jaan jaate ho ki chaabi sahi thi ya nahi -- diary mein tumhara password kahi likha nahi hota.
how_it_works: createVault: `canary = encrypt(deriveKey(masterPassword, salt), CANARY_PLAINTEXT)`. verifyMasterPassword: `candidateKey = deriveKey(candidate, record.salt)`, `decrypt(candidateKey, record.canary)` -- success/fail IS the verification.
in_this_project: `src/manager.ts::CANARY_PLAINTEXT`, `verifyMasterPassword`, `createVault`. `test/vault.test.ts`: "the wrong master password throws INVALID_MASTER_PASSWORD and issues no session". README's rules: "Unlocking derives a candidate key and tries to decrypt the canary -- AES-256-GCM's authentication tag makes a wrong key fail on its own".
advantages: No separate stored hash to keep in sync with the canary
Verification and key-derivation are the same mechanism
The exact same gate protects both unlock and changeMasterPassword's old-password check
disadvantages: If the canary plaintext/ciphertext were somehow leaked alongside enough other vaults using the SAME fixed plaintext, a determined attacker gains a tiny bit of known-plaintext information (mitigated here by salt+fresh IV ensuring no two vaults' canaries look alike)
Verification always costs one full scrypt derivation, even for an obviously wrong guess -- intentional, see the KDF question
common_mistakes: Storing a separate hash of the master password 'just in case'
Comparing decrypted canary bytes with == instead of relying on decrypt() throwing on failure
Forgetting that changeMasterPassword's old-password check must go through this same gate
follow_up_questions: Why is CANARY_PLAINTEXT a fixed, known string instead of something random per vault?
What would happen to this mechanism if AES-GCM were replaced with a non-authenticated cipher mode?
Why does changeMasterPassword's old-password check share the exact same lockout gate as unlock()?

question: What does 'an error means nothing happened' mean as a design rule in this project, and what are its deliberate exceptions?
answer_hinglish:
Default rule yeh hai: agar koi method error throw karta hai, vault ki state EXACTLY wahi reheti hai jo call se pehle thi -- kuch bhi partially apply nahi hota. Yeh property is project mein commit-after-success pattern se aati hai (pehle sab kuch prepare karo, phir ek hi `commit()` call se store confirm karo, phir hi in-memory state update karo) -- agar beech mein kuch fail ho jaaye, in-memory update ka code kabhi run hi nahi hota.

Lekin README explicitly TEEN deliberate exceptions list karta hai. Pehla: ek WRONG unlock ya changeMasterPassword attempt khud ko record KARTA hai (`failedAttempts++` inside `verifyMasterPassword`'s catch block) -- yeh exception isliye zaroori hai kyunki yeh count hi lockout ka poora point hai; agar error 'kuch nahi hua' maana jaata, lockout kabhi trigger hi nahi hota. Doosra: `VAULT_BUSY`/`ENTRY_CONFLICT` errors khud mein ek EXCEPTION hain is sense mein ki unka purpose hi hai caller ko batana "kisi aur ne pehle wo kaam kar diya" -- yeh errors deliberately silently-lost-data se better hain.

Teesra, aur sabse interesting, breach-check hai -- yeh is rule ka EXACT OPPOSITE hai: ek real failure (provider down, timeout, open circuit) ko deliberately SWALLOW kiya jaata hai (`breached: null`), error nahi throw hota, aur save FIR BHI succeed hota hai. README mein likha hai: "the opposite instinct from 'an error means nothing happened,' deliberately." Yeh dikhata hai ki yeh rule koi blind dogma nahi hai -- jab-jab zaroorat ho, deliberately override kiya gaya hai, aur har baar reasoning documented hai.
why_needed: Bina is rule ke, partial failures silently corrupt state kar sakte hain -- jaise half-re-encrypted vault, ya lost entry. Rule ko strictly follow karna predictability deta hai; exceptions ko explicitly justify karna zaroori hai taaki woh accidental bugs na lagein.
real_world_analogy: Bank transaction: agar transfer fail ho, paisa dono accounts mein wapas original state mein hona chahiye (rule). Lekin ek failed PIN attempt KHUD record hota hai (exception, security ke liye) chahe transfer kuch na kare. Aur agar fraud-check service down ho, transaction fir bhi complete ho jaata hai bina fraud-check block kiye (doosra exception, availability ke liye).
how_it_works: Commit-then-apply pattern: koi bhi mutating method pehle sab prepare karta hai, `await this.commit(...)` karta hai, aur SIRF commit succeed hone ke baad hi `record.entries.set(...)` jaisa in-memory apply karta hai. Error beech mein aaye toh apply line kabhi reach nahi hoti.
in_this_project: `src/manager.ts::verifyMasterPassword` (lockout exception), `claimEntryOp`/`VAULT_BUSY` aur `updateEntry`'s version check/`ENTRY_CONFLICT` (second exception), `src/breach-checker.ts::BreachChecker.check` (third, opposite exception). README.md 'The rules' section has this exact wording.
advantages: Caller can reason simply: error means safely retry, success means it really happened
Each exception is independently justified and tested, not an accidental leak
The rule itself catches accidental partial-state bugs during development (mutation testing specifically targets this)
disadvantages: Three exceptions means a reader must memorize them individually; the rule is not perfectly uniform
A caller who blindly assumes EVERY error means nothing happened could mishandle a VAULT_BUSY/ENTRY_CONFLICT retry if they do not realize their own stale read needs refetching first
common_mistakes: Treating ENTRY_CONFLICT as 'nothing happened' and blindly retrying with stale data instead of re-reading first
Making breach-check failures throw and block the save, defeating the whole point of the opposite exception
Forgetting to record a failed attempt, which would silently disable lockout
follow_up_questions: Why does a failed breach-check specifically break this rule instead of just being another VAULT_BUSY-style informative error?
What would happen to lockout if failed attempts were NOT recorded on error?
Can you think of another place in this codebase where this rule could have been violated by accident?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Strict 'nothing happened' simplifies retry logic for callers (error is usually safe to retry blindly), lekin teen exceptions ke liye alag-alag justification aur dedicated test chahiye, warna woh silent correctness bugs ban jaate.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar koi caller ENTRY_CONFLICT ko bhi 'nothing happened, safe retry' maan le aur apna stale local copy dobara bhej de, woh apne hi stale data se overwrite kar sakta hai dusre operation ke latest state ko -- jabki ENTRY_CONFLICT ka poora point hi hai 'pehle fresh read karo'.
advanced.alternatives: Kuch systems har attempt (success AND failure) ko audit log karte hain; yahan sirf lockout ke specific purpose ke liye failed unlock attempts record hoti hain, general audit trail nahi.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Lockout ka failedAttempts counter abhi single in-memory process mein hai, ek vault ke liye theek hai. Agar yeh system multiple server instances par horizontally scale ho, yeh counter shared store (Redis jaisa) mein move karna padega, warna attacker alag-alag instance hit karke lockout bypass kar sakta hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Sensitive operations (unlock attempts, shares, rotations) ke liye structured audit logging add karo, separate rakho is error-means-nothing-happened invariant se, taaki security visibility mile bina correctness contract tode.

question: How does the lockout mechanism work after repeated wrong master-password attempts?
answer_hinglish:
Lockout bahut simple counter-based mechanism hai. Har wrong attempt par `record.failedAttempts++` hota hai. Jab yeh count `MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS` (5) tak reach kar jaaye, `record.lockedUntil = clock.now() + LOCKOUT_MS` (30 seconds) set ho jaata hai. Jab tak `lockedUntil` future mein hai, koi bhi unlock attempt -- chahe password SAHI hi ho -- `LOCKED_OUT` error deta hai, password check tak nahi hota.

Cooldown khatam hone ke baad (`clock.now() >= lockedUntil`), `verifyMasterPassword` automatically `lockedUntil = null` aur `failedAttempts = 0` reset karta hai, aur phir normal tarike se password evaluate karta hai -- matlab ek fresh wrong attempt phir se `INVALID_MASTER_PASSWORD` dega, `LOCKED_OUT` nahi, kyunki counter reset ho gaya hai. Successful unlock bhi counter ko reset karta hai, taaki legit user occasional typo ke baad bhi stuck na ho jaaye.

Sabse important part: `changeMasterPassword` ka OWN old-password check bhi EXACT same `verifyMasterPassword` function se guzarta hai jo `unlock()` use karta hai. Yeh deliberate hai -- agar alag gate hota, toh woh ek 'unrated side door' ban jaata jahan attacker lockout bypass karke password guess kar sakta. Injectable `Clock` iska poora testing without sleep enable karta hai -- test exactly `LOCKOUT_MS - 1` aur `LOCKOUT_MS` boundary par check karte hain.
why_needed: Bina lockout, master password unlimited offline-speed attempts se guess kiya ja sakta hai. Lockout har wrong try par ek real-time cost lagata hai, jo brute-force ko impractical banata hai.
real_world_analogy: ATM card jo 3 galat PIN attempt ke baad block ho jaata hai kuch time ke liye -- chahe chautha attempt sahi PIN ho, machine turant check hi nahi karegi jab tak cooldown khatam na ho.
how_it_works: `verifyMasterPassword`: pehle check `lockedUntil` -- future hai toh `LOCKED_OUT` throw, past hai toh reset. Phir `deriveKey` + `decrypt(canary)` try karo. Fail -> `failedAttempts++`, threshold cross hua toh `lockedUntil` set. Success -> dono reset.
in_this_project: `src/manager.ts::MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS` (5), `LOCKOUT_MS` (30_000ms), `verifyMasterPassword`. `test/vault.test.ts`: "locks out after MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS consecutive wrong attempts", "the cooldown expires after LOCKOUT_MS", "once the cooldown elapses, the failed-attempt counter itself is reset", "a successful unlock resets the failed-attempt counter".
advantages: Simple counter + timestamp, no external dependency
changeMasterPassword cannot bypass the same lockout
Injectable Clock makes boundary testing exact, no flaky sleeps
disadvantages: A single in-memory counter per vault does not stop an attacker hitting many DIFFERENT ownerIds in parallel
No exponential backoff -- cooldown is always exactly LOCKOUT_MS regardless of how many times it has triggered
common_mistakes: Checking the password BEFORE checking lockedUntil (would let a correct guess sneak through during cooldown)
Forgetting to reset failedAttempts on a successful unlock
Giving changeMasterPassword its own separate, unrated attempt counter
follow_up_questions: Why does changeMasterPassword share the exact same lockout gate as unlock()?
What happens if 10,000 different ownerIds are attacked in parallel -- does this lockout help?
Why is lockedUntil reset to null exactly when the cooldown elapses, instead of just comparing timestamps every time?

question: At a conceptual level, how does the 'synchronous claim before the one await' pattern prevent races without using a lock, and what breaks if this ever moved beyond a single process?
answer_hinglish:
JavaScript ka event loop single-threaded hai -- synchronous code KABHI preempt nahi ho sakta, matlab jab tak ek function mein `await` nahi aaya, koi aur operation beech mein interleave nahi kar sakta. Is project ka pattern yeh fact exploit karta hai: har mutating operation (`addEntry`, `updateEntry`, `redeemShare`, ...) sabse pehle ek purely SYNCHRONOUS "claim" karta hai (jaise `claimEntryOp` mein `rotating` check + `pendingEntryOps++`, ya `redeemShare` mein `share.redeemedAt = now()`) -- yeh claim ek hi `await` se pehle hota hai.

Matlab do concurrent calls ke beech, check-and-set kabhi race nahi kar sakta, kyunki in dono ke beech koi await hi nahi hai jahan JS doosre call ko chance de sake. Claim ke baad ek `await` (store call / commit) hota hai, aur result ke basis par synchronous apply (success) ya release (catch block mein undo) hota hai. Yeh mutual exclusion "construction se" aata hai -- JS ke execution model ki property hai, koi mutex library ki correctness prove nahi karni padti.

Lekin yeh SIRF kaam karta hai ek single process ke andar, kyunki `rotating`/`pendingEntryOps`/`redeemedAt` sab in-memory JavaScript variables hain. Agar yeh manager multiple server instances ke peeche horizontally scale ho jaaye (load balancer ke saath), har instance apna OWN in-memory state check karega -- do alag instances DONO sochenge unhone successfully claim kar liya same vault/share par, aur `VAULT_BUSY`/`SHARE_ALREADY_REDEEMED` guarantee silently tut jaayegi, kyunki woh guarantee process-local hai, distributed nahi.
why_needed: Concurrency bugs (race conditions) debug karna sabse mehenga class of bug hai -- is pattern se race SYSTEMATICALLY impossible banta hai by construction, bina koi external locking primitive maintain kiye, jab tak single process mein ho.
real_world_analogy: Ek single bank teller jo har customer ko ek-ek kar ke serve karta hai, line mein khade sab customers ke beech kabhi interleave nahi hota kyunki ek waqt par ek hi transaction process hoti hai -- lekin agar 3 alag tellers alag counters par bina ek doosre se baat kiye kaam karein, dono ek hi account se paisa nikaal sakte hain ek saath.
how_it_works: Pattern: `claim()` (sync) -> `await asyncCall()` -> `apply()` ya `catch { release() }` (sync). Claim ke check aur increment ke beech koi await nahi hai, isliye yeh atomic hai JS ke single-threaded model mein.
in_this_project: `src/manager.ts::claimEntryOp` (entries vs rotation), `redeemShare`'s `share.redeemedAt = this.clock.now()` line (single-use shares, same shape). PLAN.md Stage 2 decisions explicitly compare yeh `17-parking-lot`'s reserve/confirm pattern se.
advantages: No lock library, no external coordination needed, zero extra latency
Correctness is a property of the language's execution model, not something to separately prove
Two different exclusion rules (entry-ops concurrent with each other, but not with rotation) expressed cheaply with two primitives
disadvantages: Only valid within a single process -- does not survive horizontal scaling
Relies entirely on convention: every new mutating method must manually call claim first, with zero type-system enforcement
common_mistakes: Putting an await before the claim call, letting a race sneak in during that earlier await
Assuming this pattern generalizes to multiple processes/instances without any changes
Forgetting to release the claim in a finally/catch on the failure path, wedging future operations
follow_up_questions: What would need to change for this claim to work correctly across multiple server instances?
Why is the breach-check call in addEntry started before the claim but awaited after it?
How does the per-entry `version` field provide a lighter-weight form of conflict detection than the vault-level claim?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Single-process in-memory claim zero-cost hai aur koi external coordination service nahi maangta, lekin yeh ONLY isliye kaam karta hai kyunki sab ek Node process ke event loop mein hai -- yeh ek distributed lock nahi hai, sirf ek process-local invariant hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar yeh manager multiple instances mein horizontally scale ho (sticky-routing ke bina), do instances dono sochenge unhone same vault/share ko successfully claim kiya -- VAULT_BUSY/SHARE_ALREADY_REDEEMED ki guarantee silently tut jaayegi, kyunki har instance ke apne alag `rotating`/`pendingEntryOps`/`shares` Maps hain.
advanced.alternatives: Real distributed deployment ke liye claim ko shared aur atomic banana padega: database row ke saath optimistic locking/version column (jo yeh project already per-entry `version` field se partially model karta hai), Redis SETNX-style distributed lock, ya saare operations ek given ownerId ke liye ek hi owning node par route karna (sharding by ownerId).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x scale par bhi single process vertically scaled fine chal sakta hai; 100x par, availability ke liye multiple instances chalane ke liye claim ko in-memory flag se ek real backing store ke atomic operation mein move karna hoga -- same tarike jaise `pendingEntryOps` ka kaam ek database transaction ya per-vault lock service ban jaana chahiye.
advanced.production_improvements: Vaults ko ownerId se specific instances mein shard karo taaki in-process claim valid rahe, ya claim ko khud VaultStore ke andar ek atomic conditional write bana do -- same claim-before-await shape rakho, par ek real atomic primitive ke backing ke saath.

question: What is envelope (hybrid) encryption conceptually, and why does sharing use RSA only to wrap a key instead of encrypting the whole entry with it?
answer_hinglish:
Envelope (hybrid) encryption ka idea yeh hai: asymmetric crypto (RSA yahan) slow hoti hai AUR sirf ek chhota payload encrypt kar sakti hai (RSA-2048 ka max payload bahut limited hai). Toh instead of RSA se poora data encrypt karne ki koshish karne ke, ek fresh one-time symmetric AES key generate karo, USSE actual data encrypt karo (fast, kisi bhi size ke liye), aur sirf us CHHOTI AES key ko RSA se recipient ke public key se wrap karo.

Recipient apni private key se sirf us chhoti wrapped key ko unwrap karta hai (fast RSA operation, chhota payload), aur phir woh AES key use kar ke actual data decrypt karta hai. Yeh exact pattern TLS aur PGP dono use karte hain -- asymmetric crypto sirf key-exchange ke liye, symmetric crypto bulk data ke liye.

Is project mein `sealForRecipient(recipientPublicKeyPem, plaintext)` yeh exact flow follow karta hai: `randomBytes(32)` se ek one-time AES key banta hai, `encrypt(oneTimeKey, plaintext)` se actual entry AES-256-GCM se encrypt hota hai (same AEAD jo baaki poore project mein use hoti hai), phir `publicEncrypt(...)` se sirf woh 32-byte key RSA-OAEP se wrap hoti hai. Result ek `ShareToken` hai jisme `wrappedKey` (chhoti) aur `blob` (poora encrypted entry) dono hote hain -- ek self-contained, portable artifact, koi live call ki zaroorat nahi.
why_needed: RSA directly se bulk data encrypt karna ya possible nahi (size limit) ya bahut slow hoga. Hybrid approach se asymmetric crypto ka fayda (secure key exchange bina shared secret pehle se hone ke) milta hai bina uski limitations ke.
real_world_analogy: Ek bada parcel bhejna hai, par tumhare paas sirf ek chhota, mehenga courier slot hai jo sirf ek chaabi bhej sakta hai. Toh parcel ko ek normal lock se band karo (fast, koi size limit nahi), aur us lock ki chaabi ko us chhote mehenge slot se bhej do -- receiver chaabi se parcel khol leta hai.
how_it_works: `sealForRecipient`: `oneTimeKey = randomBytes(32)` -> `blob = encrypt(oneTimeKey, plaintext)` (symmetric) -> `wrappedKey = publicEncrypt(recipientPublicKey, oneTimeKey)` (asymmetric, sirf 32 bytes). `openAsRecipient` reverse: private key se `oneTimeKey` unwrap, phir `decrypt(oneTimeKey, blob)`.
in_this_project: `src/sharing.ts::sealForRecipient`, `openAsRecipient`, `ShareToken` interface (`wrappedKey` + `blob`). `test/sharing.test.ts`: "sealForRecipient/openAsRecipient round-trip the exact plaintext", "the same plaintext sealed twice never produces the same token" (fresh one-time key + fresh IV every time).
advantages: No size limit on the actual shared data (symmetric does the heavy lifting)
Fast, since RSA only ever processes a tiny 32-byte payload
Same self-contained-token pattern as TLS/PGP, well-understood and battle-tested
disadvantages: Still requires generating a real RSA keypair per vault that ever shares something (~200ms, one-time cost)
Each share is a one-way, self-contained artifact -- no built-in mechanism to update/rotate what was already sealed
common_mistakes: Trying to RSA-encrypt the whole entry directly (fails or is impractically slow for larger payloads)
Reusing the same one-time AES key across multiple shares instead of generating a fresh one each time
Confusing the recipient's RSA keypair with the vault's own AES master key -- they are completely independent
follow_up_questions: Why does shareEntry need no commit or claim, unlike addEntry?
What happens if the recipientPublicKey is not a valid RSA key?
Why is a fresh one-time AES key generated per share instead of the sender reusing their own vault key?

question: Why does revokeShare() return the identical error for an unknown shareId and for someone else's shareId, and what security pattern is this an instance of?
answer_hinglish:
`revokeShare(sessionId, shareId)` ek hi condition check karta hai: `if (!share || share.ownerId !== session.ownerId)` -- dono cases mein SAME `UNKNOWN_SHARE` error throw hota hai. Caller ko kabhi yeh distinguish karne ka tareeka nahi milta ki shareId "exist hi nahi karta" ya "exist karta hai par tumhara nahi hai".

Yeh "don't-leak-existence" instinct ka instance hai -- same principle jo login systems mein use hoti hai jab ek failed login attempt par yeh nahi bataya jaata ki username galat tha ya password, sirf generic "invalid credentials" bolte hain. Agar yahan DO alag error codes hote, ek attacker apne guessed shareIds try kar ke pata laga sakta ki konsa shareId VALID hai (chahe uska nahi) vs konsa bilkul exist hi nahi karta -- yeh information attacker ke liye useful hoti hai, reconnaissance ke liye.

Practically, `shareId` already 16 random bytes (`randomBytes(16).toString("hex")`) se banta hai, toh guessing-space astronomically bada hai -- yeh error-symmetry defense-in-depth hai, primary protection shareId ki randomness hi hai. Important nuance: revoking EK already-revoked ya already-redeemed share ko harmless no-op treat kiya jaata hai, error nahi -- woh case genuine authorization failure nahi hai, sirf ek idempotent action hai. `test/share-revocation.test.ts` mein exactly yeh test hota hai: "an unknown shareId and someone else's shareId both throw UNKNOWN_SHARE".
why_needed: Error messages jo existence leak karte hain, attacker ko ek reconnaissance oracle de dete hain -- valid vs invalid targets ko distinguish karna unka pehla step hota hai kisi bhi targeted attack mein.
real_world_analogy: Ek security guard jo har bar "access denied" bolta hai, chahe tumhara card expired ho ya tumne kisi aur ka card try kiya ho -- woh kabhi nahi bolta "yeh card kabhi issue hi nahi hua" vs "yeh card kisi aur ka hai", dono responses identical hain.
how_it_works: `revokeShare`: `const share = this.shares.get(shareId); if (!share || share.ownerId !== session.ownerId) throw UNKNOWN_SHARE;`. Ek hi condition, ek hi error, dono cases cover.
in_this_project: `src/manager.ts::revokeShare`. `test/share-revocation.test.ts`: "a revoked share can no longer be redeemed", "an unknown shareId throws UNKNOWN_SHARE", "someone else's shareId also throws UNKNOWN_SHARE -- never distinguishing 'not yours' from 'does not exist'". README: "the same don't-leak-existence instinct as not telling a failed login which part was wrong".
advantages: No existence-leaking oracle for an attacker guessing shareIds
Same pattern consistently applied, same instinct as login failure messages
Revoking twice is a harmless no-op, not an extra error path to get wrong
disadvantages: A legitimate caller who made a genuine typo also gets no hint about which mistake they made
Combined with another side channel (response timing), existence could still theoretically leak -- this project does not add timing-jitter defenses
common_mistakes: Returning different error codes for 'not found' vs 'not yours'
Treating revoking an already-revoked share as an error instead of a no-op
Assuming shareId randomness alone is enough and skipping the ownership check
follow_up_questions: Where else in this project is the same don't-leak-existence instinct applied?
Why is revoking an already-redeemed share also a no-op rather than an error?
What additional defense would close a timing-based side channel here?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Do alag failure reasons ko ek error code mein combine karna debuggability ko thoda kam karta hai (legit caller yeh nahi jaan paata ki unhone typo kiya ya kisi aur ka id use kiya) security ke fayde ke liye (no enumeration oracle).
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar yeh dono cases alag error codes dete, ek attacker apne guessed shareIds (16 random bytes, already bahut hard to guess) ke saath combine karke, kisi doosre leak (jaise timing) ke saath milakar, valid-but-not-mine ko never-issued se distinguish kar sakta, guessing space ko narrow karte hue.
advanced.alternatives: Kuch systems deliberate random response-time jitter bhi add karte hain, sirf status code symmetry nahi, taaki timing side-channel bhi band ho -- yeh project woh nahi karta (shareId namespace already astronomically large hone ki wajah se).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Scale par yeh check free hai (ek line hai), load badhne se change nahi hota; yeh zyada matter karta hai jab API ko larger, less-trusted set of callers ke liye expose kiya jaaye.
advanced.production_improvements: revokeShare attempts par rate limiting add karo per caller/session, taaki brute-force enumeration attempts ko aur slow kiya ja sake, existing error-message symmetry ke upar.

question: Why is a breach check allowed to fail silently (degrading to null) instead of following this project's usual 'an error means nothing happened' rule?
answer_hinglish:
Breach-check ek non-critical, third-party-jaisi dependency hai -- agar yeh throw kar sake aur `addEntry`/`updateEntry` ko abort kar de, toh ek flaky provider ANY password save hone se rok sakta hai, jo ek 'unknown breach status' se bhi zyada bura outcome hai. Isliye `BreachChecker.check()` ko explicitly design kiya gaya hai ki yeh KABHI throw nahi karta.

Flow hai: `check()` provider call ko `CircuitBreaker.run()` ke andar wrap karta hai, jo bhi `withTimeout()` ke andar wrapped hai. Agar provider error de, timeout ho jaaye, ya circuit already open ho (fail-fast), har case mein internal exception uthta hai -- par `check()` ka OUTER try/catch sab kuch `null` (matlab unknown) mein convert kar deta hai, kuch bhi caller tak nahi throw hota. `addEntry` mein `breachCheck` promise ko claim se PEHLE start kiya jaata hai (par await nahi), aur baad mein await hone par woh kabhi fail nahi karega -- `body.breached` field `null` ban jaayega, par save FIR BHI succeed hoga.

`breached: null` deliberately `false` se ALAG hai -- `false` ka matlab "check hua aur clean mila", `null` ka matlab "pata nahi, service unreachable tha". Yeh distinction important hai kyunki UI ko "assumed safe" aur "actually verified safe" ko confuse nahi karna chahiye. Test `breach-integration.test.ts` mein directly "a broken provider never blocks a save" scenario cover hota hai.
why_needed: Password saving core feature hai; breach-checking ek add-on safety signal hai. Agar add-on feature core feature ko hi todd de jab woh khud fail ho, yeh priority inversion hai -- isliye deliberately opposite rule apply hoti hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek car ka tyre-pressure sensor kharab ho jaaye, toh car phir bhi chalti hai (core function intact) -- sirf dashboard par warning light nahi dikhegi, 'pressure unknown' ki jagah. Sensor fail hone se engine lock nahi ho jaata.
how_it_works: `check()`: `try { return await breaker.run(() => withTimeout(...)); } catch { return null; }` -- outer catch sab kuch (timeout, provider error, open circuit) null mein convert karta hai.
in_this_project: `src/breach-checker.ts::BreachChecker.check`, `src/manager.ts::addEntry` (breach check started before claim, awaited inside try). `test/breach-integration.test.ts`: "a broken provider never blocks a save". `types.ts::EntrySummary.breached` comment: "null = never checked or the breach-check service could not be reached (unknown, NOT 'assumed safe')".
advantages: A flaky third-party dependency can never block the core save flow
breached: null is an explicit, distinct state from false -- no false sense of security
Circuit breaker + timeout together stop a slow provider from even delaying every save for long
disadvantages: breached: null is a third state every caller/UI must handle correctly, not just true/false
No automatic retry/background re-check of entries left at null once the provider recovers
common_mistakes: Treating breached: null as if it means 'assumed safe' in UI code
Letting a breach-check failure propagate and block addEntry/updateEntry
Assuming the circuit breaker alone is enough without also having a per-call timeout
follow_up_questions: What is the difference between breached: false and breached: null, and why does the project distinguish them?
Why is the breach-check call started before claimEntryOp but awaited inside the try block?
How would you let a user later re-check entries that are stuck at breached: null?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Strict correctness (always know breach status) ko trade kiya gaya hai primary feature ki availability (password save) ke saath -- ek classic degrade-gracefully trade-off; cost yeh hai ki 'breached: null' ek teesra state ban jaata hai jo har caller/UI ko handle karna padta hai, sirf true/false nahi.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar breach provider extended period ke liye down ho, circuit breaker open ho jaata hai aur baaki saare subsequent checks bina provider ko call kiye hi fail-fast null ban jaate hain -- users password save karte rehte hain, sirf breach signal ke bina, jab tak provider recover na ho aur ek half-open trial succeed na ho.
advanced.alternatives: Ek stricter system breach check ko queue kar sakta hai baad ke liye (password hash-prefix store karo, async re-check later) instead of sirf give up karne ke -- yeh project automatically koi null result retry nahi karta.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 100x save volume par circuit breaker ka failureThreshold/cooldown tuning zyada matter karta hai -- bahut sensitive ho toh real transient blips unnecessarily circuit open kar dete hain; bahut lax ho toh ek genuinely-down provider ko open hone se pehle kaafi timeouts se hammer kiya jaata hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Background job jo breached: null entries ko dobara check kare jab provider healthy ho jaaye, plus circuit-state transitions par metrics/alerting, taaki ek extended outage operators ko visible ho, sirf silently degrade na ho users ke liye.

question: What fields does the internal VaultRecord interface in manager.ts actually carry, and what is each field's specific job?
answer_hinglish:
`VaultRecord` ek private, non-exported interface hai jo `src/manager.ts` ke andar hi defined hai -- yeh wahi internal shape hai jo poori vault ki in-memory state represent karta hai. Fields hain: `ownerId`, `createdAt`, `salt` (Buffer), `canary` (EncryptedBlob), `entries` (`Map<string, StoredEntry>`), `nextEntrySeq` (number, next entry ID allocate karne ke liye), `failedAttempts` aur `lockedUntil` (lockout state), `generation` (number, session-invalidation ke liye), `rotating` (boolean) aur `pendingEntryOps` (number) -- yeh dono claim mechanism ke do pillars hain, `sharingPublicKey` aur `wrappedPrivateKey` (sharing feature ka lazily-generated state).

Har field ka ek specific, deliberate purpose hai. `rotating` sirf ek rotation ke flight mein hone ko track karta hai (boolean kaafi hai kyunki EK waqt par sirf ek rotation allowed hai -- doosri `VAULT_BUSY` dega). `pendingEntryOps` ek COUNTER hai, boolean nahi, kyunki multiple entry operations SAME time par legitimately chal sakte hain (do devices do alag entries add kar rahe hain) -- yeh counter sirf rotation ko exclude karta hai, entry-ops ko ek doosre se exclude nahi karta. `generation` number hai jo har successful `changeMasterPassword` par increment hota hai -- har Session apna captured generation `requireSession` mein compare karta hai, mismatch hone par `SESSION_INVALIDATED`.

`nextEntrySeq` synchronously allocate hota hai (`e${record.nextEntrySeq++}`), isliye do concurrent adds ke IDs kabhi collide nahi karte, chahe unka commit kitna bhi der se resolve ho. `sharingPublicKey`/`wrappedPrivateKey` nullable hain kyunki har vault RSA keypair lazily generate karta hai, sirf jab pehli baar sharing use ho.
why_needed: Yeh interface na-exported hone ke bawajood poore manager.ts ka core state model hai -- iske fields ka exact purpose samajhna zaroori hai taaki koi naya method galat field manipulate na kare ya claim mechanism ko accidentally skip na kare.
real_world_analogy: Ek factory floor ka control panel jisme alag-alag switches hain: ek 'maintenance mode' switch (sirf on/off, jaise `rotating`), ek 'active workers' counter (jaise `pendingEntryOps`, kyunki multiple workers saath chal sakte hain), aur ek 'shift number' counter (jaise `generation`, jo badges invalidate karta hai jab shift badalti hai).
how_it_works: `createVault` sabhi fields ko initial values ke saath set karta hai. Mutating methods (`addEntry`, `changeMasterPassword`, etc.) sirf apne specific fields update karte hain, aur sirf commit succeed hone ke baad.
in_this_project: `src/manager.ts::VaultRecord` aur `StoredEntry` (jo `entries` Map ke values hain, apna `version` field rakhte hain conflict detection ke liye). Dekho `createVault` ka initial object literal poore shape ke liye.
advantages: Each field has exactly one clear job, making the record easy to reason about despite being mutable
rotating (bool) + pendingEntryOps (counter) gives two DIFFERENT exclusion rules cheaply
generation as a simple incrementing number avoids needing to eagerly walk every session on rotation
disadvantages: Entirely in-memory -- nothing here survives a process restart, by design for this project's scope
A future contributor could add a new mutating field and forget to wire it through the claim/commit flow correctly, since there's no compiler enforcement of that discipline
common_mistakes: Reading record.salt/record.canary directly inside commit() instead of taking them as explicit parameters
Using a boolean instead of a counter for pendingEntryOps, which would wrongly serialize concurrent entry ops against each other
Forgetting to decrement pendingEntryOps in a finally block, permanently wedging rotation
follow_up_questions: Why is pendingEntryOps a counter instead of a boolean?
What would happen if generation were never incremented on a successful rotation?
Why are sharingPublicKey and wrappedPrivateKey nullable instead of generated eagerly at createVault time?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: rotating aur pendingEntryOps ko do alag primitives (bool + counter) rakhna, ek generic 'busy' lock ke bajaye, rotation aur entry-ops ko DIFFERENT exclusion rules dene deta hai (multiple concurrent entry-ops theek hain, par rotation ke saath koi bhi nahi) -- single mutually-exclusive lock needlessly do adds ko bhi ek doosre se serialize kar deta.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar `pendingEntryOps` sirf happy path mein decrement hota (finally mein nahi), ek thrown error mid-operation counter ko permanently stuck chhod deta zero se upar -- yeh exactly wajah hai ki finally block exist karta hai addEntry/updateEntry/deleteEntry/getSharingPublicKey mein.
advanced.alternatives: Ek single 'busy: boolean' flag simpler hota, par woh do legitimate concurrent adds ko bhi ek doosre ke against block kar deta, jabki 'two devices adding at once' test explicitly prove karta hai ki dono succeed hone chahiye.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: In-memory counters O(1) hain regardless of scale; real scaling limit yeh hai ki VaultRecord aur uska entries Map poore ek process ki memory mein rehte hain, toh har vault ka data us process ki RAM se capped hai aur restart par lost ho jaata hai.
advanced.production_improvements: generation/rotating state ko real VaultStore-backed system mein entries ke saath persist karo, taaki mid-rotation crash recover/detect ho sake, sirf process memory mein hone ke bajaye.

question: What does the internal Session interface store per unlocked session, and why does each field exist?
answer_hinglish:
`Session` bhi `manager.ts` ke andar hi defined, non-exported interface hai -- ek unlock call ka result represent karta hai. Fields: `sessionId` (public identifier), `ownerId` (konse vault ke liye hai), `key` (Buffer, derived AES key), `generation` (number, vault ke generation ki snapshot unlock ke waqt), aur `lastActivityAt` (number, idle-timeout tracking).

`key` ko Session mein store karna important decision hai -- isse har call par master password dobara derive nahi karna padta (jo deliberately slow hai, scrypt ki wajah se). Device apna master password bhi nahi retain karta, sirf yeh derived key session ke life-time tak rehta hai, jo ek real-world behaviour ke similar hai jaha app unlock hone ke baad password dobara nahi poochta.

`generation` field unlock ke exact moment ka vault generation capture karta hai. Agar baad mein koi `changeMasterPassword` call ho jaaye, vault ka generation increment ho jaata hai, par is session ka captured generation PURANA reh jaata hai -- `requireSession` mein `record.generation !== session.generation` check se yeh mismatch detect hota hai aur `SESSION_INVALIDATED` throw hota hai, session ko lazily delete kar ke. `lastActivityAt` sirf `requireSession` ke successful path par update hota hai (`isSessionActive` ise NEVER touch karta -- woh pure read hai), isliye idle-auto-lock reliably kaam karta hai.
why_needed: Session ka shape exactly decide karta hai ki multi-device support, session-invalidation-on-rotation, aur idle-timeout teeno features kaise independently kaam karte hain ek hi object ke andar, bina ek doosre ko interfere kiye.
real_world_analogy: Ek hotel room keycard jisme ek room number (ownerId), ek activation-date-stamp (generation, jo expire ho jaata hai agar hotel apna master lock system reset kare), aur ek 'last swiped' timestamp (lastActivityAt, jo housekeeping ko batata hai room abhi active hai ya nahi) encoded hote hain.
how_it_works: `unlock()`: `this.sessions.set(sessionId, { sessionId, ownerId, key, generation: record.generation, lastActivityAt: this.clock.now() })`. `requireSession` dono `generation` aur `lastActivityAt` ko validate karta hai aur `lastActivityAt` ko refresh karta hai on success.
in_this_project: `src/manager.ts::Session`, `unlock`, `requireSession`. `test/session-idle-timeout.test.ts`: "multiple sessions on the same vault have INDEPENDENT idle clocks", "a freshly unlocked session starts its idle clock at the moment of unlock, not some earlier time".
advantages: Storing the derived key avoids re-running the deliberately-slow KDF on every call
generation capture makes session invalidation a lazy O(1) comparison, no eager walk needed
Each session's own lastActivityAt gives multi-device users independent idle clocks
disadvantages: The key lives in process memory for the session's whole lifetime -- JavaScript cannot reliably zero it out on lock()
Sessions are entirely in-memory; nothing survives a restart, same documented limitation as the rest of this project
common_mistakes: Re-deriving the key from the master password on every call instead of storing it once per session
Forgetting to capture generation at unlock time, which would make SESSION_INVALIDATED impossible to detect
Letting isSessionActive bump lastActivityAt, which would defeat the idle-timeout feature
follow_up_questions: Why is the derived key stored on the session instead of the master password itself?
What would happen if two devices shared one Session object instead of each getting their own?
Why is generation compared by equality rather than by 'is session's generation >= record's'?

question: What does the internal ShareGrant interface track, and why does it live in a manager-wide map instead of inside a VaultRecord?
answer_hinglish:
`ShareGrant` manager.ts ka teesra non-exported internal interface hai. Fields: `shareId` (opaque tracking reference, secret NAHI hai -- sirf grant ko dhoondhne ke liye, iske sath koi crypto nahi hoti), `ownerId` (sirf WOH vault ise revoke kar sakta hai), `revoked` (boolean), aur `redeemedAt` (`number | null` -- non-null ban jaana hi single-use claim hai).

Yeh grants ek alag, manager-level `shares: Map<string, ShareGrant>` mein store hote hain, `sessions` ki tarah, NA ki kisi VaultRecord ke andar. Reasoning README mein explicitly di gayi hai: yeh bookkeeping hai EK TRANSACTION ke BARE MEIN do vaults ke beech, kisi EK vault ka content nahi hai. Comment code mein bhi likha hai: "like Session, not vault content: it never goes through VaultStore, and does not survive a restart".

Yeh design choice directly affect karta hai ki revocation aur single-use kaise implement hote hain. Kyunki yeh manager-level hai, `revokeShare` ko sirf `this.shares.get(shareId)` lookup karna padta hai, kisi specific vault ke andar search nahi karna padta. Aur kyunki yeh VaultStore se nahi guzarta, ismein koi commit/claim machinery nahi lagti jaisi entries ke liye lagti hai -- `redeemedAt` ki synchronous assignment hi poora claim hai, bilkul `claimEntryOp` jaisa shape, par alag resource ke liye.
why_needed: Share grants poore sharing-revocation-single-use feature ka foundation hain -- inka exact shape samajhna zaroori hai yeh samajhne ke liye ki revoke aur redeem kaise ek doosre se interact karte hain race conditions mein.
real_world_analogy: Ek courier company ka central tracking system jo har parcel ka delivery-grant track karta hai (kisne bheja, deliver hua ya nahi, cancel hua ya nahi) -- yeh tracking record kisi EK sender ke ghar mein nahi rakha jaata, central office mein rakha jaata hai, kyunki yeh dono parties ke beech ki transaction ke bare mein hai.
how_it_works: `shareEntry`: `this.shares.set(shareId, { shareId, ownerId: session.ownerId, revoked: false, redeemedAt: null })`. `redeemShare`: `share.redeemedAt = this.clock.now()` (the claim). `revokeShare`: `share.revoked = true`.
in_this_project: `src/manager.ts::ShareGrant`, `shareEntry`, `revokeShare`, `redeemShare`. `test/share-revocation.test.ts`: "a share is single-use (SHARE_ALREADY_REDEEMED on the second attempt, no duplicate entry)", "two concurrent redemptions of the same token: exactly one succeeds".
advantages: Manager-level map keeps lookup simple: no need to search inside any specific vault's entries
Consistent with the existing 'sessions' pattern -- same reasoning, same place
No VaultStore/commit machinery needed since grants never persist
disadvantages: Share grants do not survive a process restart, same documented limitation as sessions
shareId being just a lookup key (not itself a secret) means its only real protection is the crypto inside the token plus this grant's revoked/redeemedAt state
common_mistakes: Storing share grants inside VaultRecord, which would complicate lookups and conflate transaction metadata with vault content
Treating shareId as if it were secret and sufficient on its own to open the entry
Forgetting that redeemedAt must be set SYNCHRONOUSLY, before any await, to keep single-use correct
follow_up_questions: Why is shareId not itself a secret, and what would happen if it were treated as one?
What is the exact sequence of checks in redeemShare before the claim happens?
Why does revoking an already-redeemed share succeed as a no-op instead of throwing?

question: Walk through exactly what requireSession() checks, in what order, and explain why idle-timeout logic specifically lives there and nowhere else.
answer_hinglish:
`requireSession(sessionId)` ek private helper hai jo sequentially checks karta hai: (1) `this.sessions.get(sessionId)` -- missing hua toh `UNKNOWN_SESSION`. (2) Vault record lookup karo; agar record missing hai YA `record.generation !== session.generation`, session ko `this.sessions.delete(sessionId)` se lazily cleanup kar do aur `SESSION_INVALIDATED` throw karo. (3) `this.clock.now() - session.lastActivityAt > this.sessionIdleTimeoutMs` check karo -- true hua toh phir se session delete karo aur `SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT` throw karo. (4) Sab pass hua toh `session.lastActivityAt = this.clock.now()` set karo (yehi activity-reset hai) aur session return karo.

Yeh method EK choke point hai -- `getEntry`, `listEntries`, `addEntry`, `updateEntry`, `deleteEntry`, `getSharingPublicKey`, `shareEntry`, `revokeShare`, `redeemShare` -- sab inhi line se shuru hote hain: `const session = this.requireSession(sessionId)`. Isliye idle-auto-lock logic yahin reh sakta hai -- yeh EK jagah hai jahan check bhi hota hai aur reset bhi, naye method ko kuch bhi yaad nahi rakhna padta.

`isSessionActive`, iske contrast mein, yeh SAME checks duplicate karta hai (alive + generation + idle) par `requireSession` ko kabhi call nahi karta aur `lastActivityAt` KABHI nahi bumpta -- yeh deliberate hai, kyunki ek status-check jo poll karke session ko zinda rakh sake, poore idle-timeout feature ka point hi defeat kar degi. Ek interesting mutation (IT4 `README` ke mutation-check table mein) exactly yeh target karta tha: 'using a session never resets its idle clock' -- yeh pakdi gayi.
why_needed: Session-based security checks ko multiple jagah duplicate karna bug-prone hota hai -- koi naya method likhte waqt koi check bhool sakta hai. Ek single choke point se yeh possibility hi eliminate ho jaati hai, jab tak convention follow ho.
real_world_analogy: Ek office building ka single turnstile entry jisse har employee guzarta hai, jahan badge validity aur last-swipe time dono check hote hain ek hi jagah -- alag-alag doors par alag security logic rakhne se koi door miss ho sakta hai.
how_it_works: Sequential checks: lookup -> generation match -> idle deadline -> reset clock -> return. Lazy cleanup dono failure paths (SESSION_INVALIDATED, SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT) mein hota hai, taaki session ever phir se valid na ban sake.
in_this_project: `src/manager.ts::requireSession`, `isSessionActive`. `test/session-idle-timeout.test.ts`: "isSessionActive is a pure read: calling it repeatedly does NOT itself reset the idle clock", "an idle-timed-out session is cleaned up: isSessionActive reflects it immediately, and it never becomes valid again".
advantages: Every new session-based method gets correct generation-check AND idle-timeout behavior for free
isSessionActive remaining a pure read preserves the entire point of the idle-timeout feature
Lazy cleanup on both failure paths means a dead session can never be revived
disadvantages: requireSession bundles several responsibilities (lookup, generation check, idle check, idle reset, cleanup) into one function, which a careless future edit could partially break
A future method that reads this.sessions.get() directly instead of calling requireSession would silently skip all of this
common_mistakes: Adding a new session-based method that bypasses requireSession for 'simplicity'
Letting isSessionActive bump lastActivityAt (would let polling keep a session alive forever)
Checking idle timeout before the generation check, which could give a confusing error for an already-invalidated session
follow_up_questions: What specific bug would appear if isSessionActive also reset the idle clock?
Why does a generation mismatch delete the session immediately rather than leaving it for later cleanup?
How would you add a new session-based method safely, guaranteeing it goes through this choke point?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Dono invalidation check aur idle-timeout check/reset ko ek jagah centralize karna matlab har naya session-based API method correct behaviour free mein paata hai sirf requireSession call karke -- cost yeh hai ki yeh ek function kai responsibilities bundle karta hai (lookup, generation check, idle check, idle reset, lazy cleanup), jo ek less careful review future mein miss kar sakta hai jab naya check add karna ho.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar future mein koi contributor ek naya session-based method add kare jo directly `this.sessions.get(sessionId)` read kare instead of requireSession call karne ke, woh silently generation-invalidation CHECK aur idle timeout DONO skip kar degi -- exactly woh bug jo yeh single-choke-point design impossible banana chahta hai by construction, jab tak convention actually follow ho.
advanced.alternatives: Ek decorator/middleware jo har session-taking method ko wrap kare kuch languages mein possible hai, par TypeScript/JS mein koi clean built-in method-decorator-with-easy-private-state-access pattern nahi hai jo itna lightweight ho jitna ek private helper call karna.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Lazy expiry ka matlab hai idle sessions `sessions` Map mein memory consume karte rehte hain apne next touch tak (ya forever, agar kabhi touch na ho) -- 100x user base par, bahut saare sessions jo ek baar open ho kar abandon ho gaye, process bahut saare stale Session objects accumulate kar sakta hai; ek background sweep (simplicity ko trade karke bounded memory ke liye) is scale par consider karne layak ban jaata hai, chahe abhi is project ke scale par zaroori nahi hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Ek optional periodic sweep add karo (correctness-critical lazy check se alag, sirf memory bound ke liye) jo sessions ko evict kare jo apne timeout se bahut aage idle hain, aur session count/age metrics expose karo taaki idle-session memory growth observable ho pehle ki woh problem bane.

question: What do the private helpers requireVault() and requireEntry() do, and why are they written as simple lookup-or-throw functions?
answer_hinglish:
Dono bahut simple, chhote helpers hain, par poore manager.ts mein repeatedly use hote hain. `requireVault(ownerId)`: `this.vaults.get(ownerId)` karo, agar `undefined` mile toh `UNKNOWN_OWNER` throw karo, warna record return karo. `requireEntry(record, entryId)`: `record.entries.get(entryId)` karo, agar `undefined` mile toh `UNKNOWN_ENTRY` throw karo, warna stored entry return karo.

Yeh pattern -- "lookup, missing hone par throw, warna return" -- itna common hai is codebase mein ki ise ek helper function mein factor karna obvious choice hai. Har public method jo kisi vault ya entry ki zaroorat rakhta hai (jaise `getEntry`, `addEntry`, `updateEntry`, `exportVault`, `getVault`) isi ek helper ko call karta hai, iska matlab error message aur error CODE dono consistent rehte hain har jagah -- kahin `UNKNOWN_OWNER` kahin kuch aur nahi hoga, ek hi jagah se nikalta hai.

Agar yeh helpers na hote, har method apna khud `if (!record) throw ...` likhta, jo (1) duplicate code hota, (2) koi method galti se yeh check bhool sakta aur `record.someField` access karte waqt ek raw `TypeError` throw karta (instead of ek clean `PasswordManagerError`). Yeh chhota sa refactor is project ke bade "an error means nothing happened, with a clean error code" philosophy ko consistently enforce karta hai bina har jagah dobara likhe.
why_needed: Consistency aur safety ke liye -- har jagah same existence-check manually likhne se duplicate code aur chhuta hua check dono ka risk hota hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek library ka front-desk jo har request par pehle check karta hai 'kya yeh member card valid hai' -- yeh check ek hi desk par hota hai, har alag counter apna khud ka validity-check nahi likhta.
how_it_works: `requireVault`: `const record = this.vaults.get(ownerId); if (!record) throw UNKNOWN_OWNER; return record;`. `requireEntry`: same shape, `record.entries.get(entryId)` ke saath, `UNKNOWN_ENTRY` ke saath.
in_this_project: `src/manager.ts::requireVault`, `requireEntry`. Called from `getVault`, `unlock`, `addEntry`, `getEntry`, `listEntries`, `updateEntry`, `deleteEntry`, `getSharingPublicKey`, `shareEntry`, `redeemShare`, `changeMasterPassword`, `exportVault` -- almost every public method.
advantages: Consistent error code and message everywhere a vault or entry is looked up
Removes duplicate existence-check code from every public method
Impossible to accidentally access an undefined record/entry and get a raw TypeError instead of a clean error
disadvantages: None meaningful at this project's scale -- the trade-off is purely positive for a pattern repeated this often
common_mistakes: Writing a fresh existence check inline in a new method instead of reusing requireVault/requireEntry
Forgetting the check entirely and letting a TypeError leak out instead of a PasswordManagerError
follow_up_questions: Why does requireEntry take the already-looked-up record as a parameter instead of looking up the vault itself too?
What would a caller see if requireVault simply returned undefined instead of throwing?
Where does requireSession fit relative to requireVault in the typical call sequence of a method like addEntry?

question: What exactly does claimEntryOp() do internally, and why must it run with zero awaits before it inside the calling method?
answer_hinglish:
