`claimEntryOp(record)` ka poora body do lines hai: `if (record.rotating) throw VAULT_BUSY;` phir `record.pendingEntryOps++`. Dono lines COMPLETELY synchronous hain -- koi await, koi Promise, kuch nahi. Yehi uski poori power hai.

Kyunki JS synchronous code ko preempt nahi kar sakta, jab yeh function kisi mutating method (`addEntry`, `updateEntry`, `deleteEntry`, `getSharingPublicKey`) ke andar sabse PEHLE statement ke roop mein call hota hai -- koi await uske PEHLE nahi hona chahiye, chahe woh breach-check jaisi async step hi ho -- tab check-aur-increment ke beech koi doosra operation interleave nahi kar sakta. Yeh guarantee TABHI tak sahi hai jab tak koi await claimEntryOp se pehle na aaye.

`addEntry` mein yeh specifically dikhta hai: breach-check promise ko START kiya jaata hai (`const breachCheck = this.breachChecker.check(password)`) PAR AWAIT nahi kiya jaata, phir `claimEntryOp(record)` call hota hai, aur SIRF uske baad `await breachCheck` hota hai andar try block mein. PLAN.md Stage 3 decisions mein yeh EXACTLY call out kiya gaya hai: "The breach-check call starts (but is not awaited) before any claim... This keeps claimEntryOp's 'run synchronously, before any await' invariant from stage 2 completely intact." Agar koi galti se `await this.breachChecker.check(password)` ko claimEntryOp se PEHLE likh deta, ek rotation uss await ke beech mein sneak kar sakta tha, aur claim apna purpose kho deta.
why_needed: Yeh invariant hi poore race-prevention mechanism ki foundation hai -- isko todna (even accidentally, naye feature add karte waqt) poore claim-based design ko silently invalid bana deta.
real_world_analogy: Ek race mein starting gun chalne SE PEHLE koi bhi runner line nahi cross kar sakta -- par agar starter khud thoda ruk jaaye gun chalaane ke BAAD kisi aur kaam mein (ek 'await' jaisa gap), koi runner cheat kar sakta hai usi gap mein.
how_it_works: `claimEntryOp`: `if (record.rotating) throw VAULT_BUSY; record.pendingEntryOps++;` -- called as literally the first statement, synchronously, before any await in the calling method.
in_this_project: `src/manager.ts::claimEntryOp`, `addEntry` (breach-check started-not-awaited pattern). `test/concurrency.test.ts`: "addEntry started WHILE a rotation is in flight is rejected with VAULT_BUSY", "changeMasterPassword started WHILE an addEntry is in flight is rejected with VAULT_BUSY".
advantages: Zero-cost, zero-dependency mutual exclusion for this one process
The invariant is simple enough to state in one sentence and verify by inspection
Explicitly survived stage 3's added async complexity (breach-check) without weakening
disadvantages: Entirely convention-based -- nothing in the type system enforces 'no await before this call'
A future refactor that reorders statements could silently reintroduce the exact race this prevents
common_mistakes: Awaiting the breach-check promise before calling claimEntryOp
Calling claimEntryOp after some other async validation step instead of as the very first synchronous action
Forgetting to decrement pendingEntryOps in a finally block on every exit path
follow_up_questions: What would the concurrency.test.ts 'addEntry vs rotation' test observe differently if the await came before the claim?
Could a linter rule enforce 'claimEntryOp must be the first statement' automatically?
Why does getSharingPublicKey also need this same claim, even though it is not adding an entry?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Claim ko literally pehla synchronous statement banana (input validation ke baad, jo khud bhi sync hai) simple hai aur koi locking library nahi maangta, par yeh ek convention hai jo har method ko haath se honor karna padta hai -- koi type-system enforcement nahi hai ki future mein koi method correctly apne pehle await se pehle claimEntryOp call kare.
advanced.failure_scenarios: PLAN.md ka Stage 3 decision explicitly call out karta hai ki addEntry ka breach-check call START (await nahi) hota hai claim se pehle, specifically isliye ki stage 3 ka naya async step accidentally claim se pehle ek await na introduce kar de aur stage 2 ka established invariant na toote.
advanced.alternatives: Ek linter rule ya ek wrapper jo force kare 'claim must be the first statement' ise convention aur code-review ke bajaye construction se catch kar sakta, extra tooling complexity ki cost par ek project is size ke liye.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Yeh claim O(1) aur process-local hai, toh scale ke saath expensive nahi hota; jo scale par change hota hai (multiple server instances) woh yeh hai ki yeh akela kaafi nahi reh jaata, same point jo broader claim-before-await discussion mein hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Code-review checklist item ya automated test pattern add karo (mutation testing already partially isko cover karta hai, jaise S6/S7 breaks) specifically assert karte hue ki claimEntryOp har mutating method mein kisi bhi await se PEHLE aata hai, taaki future refactor silently is invariant ko na tod sake.

question: How does the private commit() method build the PersistedVault snapshot it hands to the store, and why are all its fields passed explicitly instead of read directly off `record`?
answer_hinglish:
`commit(record, fields)` ek explicit `fields` object leta hai -- `{ salt, canary, entries, sharingPublicKey, wrappedPrivateKey }` -- aur usse ek `PersistedVault` snapshot banata hai: `salt` Buffer ko base64 string mein convert karta hai, `entries` array (StoredEntry[]) ko `PersistedEntry` shape mein map karta hai (`id`, `blob`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `lastUsedAt` -- `version` field CHHOD diya jaata hai, kyunki woh purely in-memory conflict-detection ke liye hai, persist karne ki zaroorat nahi). Phir `withTimeout((signal) => this.store.persist(snapshot, signal), this.commitTimeoutMs)` call karta hai.

Sabse important design decision yahan yeh hai ki commit() KABHI `record.salt`, `record.canary`, etc. seedha nahi padhta -- caller (`addEntry`, `updateEntry`, `changeMasterPassword`, `getSharingPublicKey`) ko yeh SAB EXPLICITLY pass karna padta hai, chahe woh unchanged hi ho (jaise `addEntry` mein `salt: record.salt, canary: record.canary` unchanged pass hote hain). Yeh deliberate hai: isse koi commit kabhi accidentally ek STALE salt/canary ko FRESH entries ke saath mix nahi kar sakta, ya vice versa.

Yeh exactly woh gap tha jo mutation S22 ne pakda: `changeMasterPassword` in-memory vault ka salt/canary correctly update kar raha tha, PAR usi commit ko handed snapshot OLD salt/canary use kar sakta tha agar wiring galat hoti -- koi existing test kabhi yeh check nahi karta tha ki ACTUALLY durably kya saved hua, sirf in-memory result baad mein. Ek crash exactly commit ke baad (in-memory assignment se pehle) ek durably-saved vault chhod deta jiske entries naye key se encrypted hote par salt/canary PURANE ko point karte -- na purane na naye password se readable. README mein test ka fix documented hai: store ka last-persisted snapshot directly inspect karna.
why_needed: Ek commit function jo implicit state read kare, future refactors mein silently galat combination persist kar sakta hai -- explicit parameters yeh class of bug by-construction impossible banate hain.
real_world_analogy: Ek form jisme tumhe HAR field manually fill karna padta hai, chahe woh "same as before" hi ho, instead of form khud assume kar le ki kuch fields automatically purani values se bhar jayengi -- isse koi accidentally stale aur fresh data ka mismatch nahi bhar sakta.
how_it_works: `commit(record, fields)`: snapshot build karo `fields` se (salt.toString("base64"), entries.map(...), etc.), phir `withTimeout(signal => store.persist(snapshot, signal), commitTimeoutMs)` await karo.
in_this_project: `src/manager.ts::commit`, `src/store.ts::PersistedVault`. README's "Mutation checks" section, S22: "A persisted-snapshot bug: changeMasterPassword was correctly updating the in-memory vault's salt/canary, but the snapshot handed to the store for that same commit could have used the OLD salt/canary".
advantages: Impossible to accidentally mix a stale salt/canary with fresh entries, or vice versa
Every caller's intent is visible at the call site -- no hidden implicit reads
The timeout wrapper means a hung store call cannot leave this commit pending forever
disadvantages: Every caller must remember to pass ALL five fields even when most are unchanged, which is some repetition
Passing unchanged fields explicitly can look redundant to a reader unfamiliar with why this pattern exists
common_mistakes: Reading record.salt/record.canary directly inside commit() instead of requiring the caller to pass them
Forgetting to include wrappedPrivateKey/sharingPublicKey in a commit, silently dropping sharing state
Assuming the in-memory result after commit() tells you what was actually durably persisted
